## Introduction

For this assignment, I selected three Microsoft Press books covering Microsoft Office 2016. Each book is represented by its title, authors, publication year, publisher, and ISBN. One of the selected books has multiple authors, satisfying the assignment requirements.

The book information is organized into two files: an HTML table and a JSON file. Both contain the same records and attributes, allowing me to examine how R handles different data formats. I will use the `rvest` and `jsonlite` packages to import the files, convert their contents into data frames, and compare the results using `identical()`. The process and findings will be documented in this Quarto report.

## Books Chosen

The following three Microsoft Press books were selected for the dataset.

| Title | Authors | Year | Publisher | ISBN |
|----|----|---:|----|----|
| [Microsoft Office 2016 Step by Step](https://www.microsoftpressstore.com/store/microsoft-office-2016-step-by-step-9780735699236) | Joan Lambert, Curtis Frye | 2015 | Microsoft Press | 978-0-7356-9923-6 |
| [Microsoft Excel 2016 Step by Step](https://www.microsoftpressstore.com/store/microsoft-excel-2016-step-by-step-9780735698802) | Curtis Frye | 2015 | Microsoft Press | 978-0-7356-9880-2 |
| [Microsoft Word 2016 Step by Step](https://www.microsoftpressstore.com/store/microsoft-word-2016-step-by-step-9780735697775) | Joan Lambert | 2015 | Microsoft Press | 978-0-7356-9777-5 |

## Importing HTML Data

The HTML file contains a table with the selected book information. The file is hosted on GitHub and imported using the `rvest` package.

```{r html import}
#| label: import-html

library(rvest)

html_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmald1987/DATA607_HTML_JSON/refs/heads/main/books.html"

books_html <- read_html(html_url) |>
  html_element("table") |>
  html_table() |>
  as.data.frame()

knitr::kable(
  books_html,
  caption = "Books Imported from HTML"
)
```

## Importing JSON Data

The JSON file represents the same three books as structured records. The file is also hosted on GitHub and imported using `jsonlite`.

```{r json import}
#| label: import-json

library(jsonlite)

json_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmald1987/DATA607_HTML_JSON/refs/heads/main/books.json"

books_json <- fromJSON(json_url) |>
  as.data.frame()

knitr::kable(
  books_json,
  caption = "Books Imported from JSON"
)
```

## Comparing the Data Frames

After importing both files, I will standardize the column names, column order, and data types before comparing the data frames.

```{r compare DF }


# Standardize column names
names(books_html) <- tolower(names(books_html))
names(books_json) <- tolower(names(books_json))

# Match column order
books_html <- books_html[
  , names(books_json), drop = FALSE
]

# Standardize data types
books_html[] <- lapply(books_html, as.character)
books_json[] <- lapply(books_json, as.character)

# Compare the data frames
comparison <- identical(books_html, books_json)

comparison
```

## Results

The comparison checks whether both imported data frames contain identical values after standardizing their structures.

```{r results}

if (comparison) {
  cat("The HTML and JSON data frames are identical.")
} else {
  cat("The HTML and JSON data frames are not identical.")
}
```

## Conclusion

This assignment explored how the same book information can be stored in HTML and JSON and imported into R. Using `rvest` and `jsonlite`, both files were converted into data frames for comparison.

After standardizing the column order and data types, `identical()` returned **`r comparison`**. `r if (comparison) "This confirms that both files produced identical data frames after standardization." else "This indicates that differences remain between the imported data frames and require further examination."`

The exercise provided practical experience working with both formats and validating data consistency across different sources.
